clinicalScope: Breech presentation in pregnant women at term or near term presenting to low‑resource obstetric services in East Africa
title: Breech Presentation
subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
summary: Breech presentation is when the fetal buttocks or feet present first. It occurs in 3‑4% of term pregnancies and requires careful diagnosis and planning for safe delivery, especially where resources are limited.

sections.p: A breech presentation is any fetal position where the presenting part is the buttocks, feet, or a combination, rather than the skull.
b: Firm, round head felt high in the fundus (ballotable) suggests breech
Soft, broad presenting part palpable above the maternal umbilicus
Ultrasound (if available) confirms fetal orientation and type

sections.p: Breech is classified by the relationship of hips and knees, which guides delivery planning.
b: Frank breech – hips flexed, knees extended (≈65% of breeches)
Complete breech – hips and knees flexed
Footling/incomplete breech – one or both feet presenting

sections.p: Most breeches are idiopathic, but several maternal, fetal and uterine factors increase risk.
b: Prematurity (<37 weeks) – higher incidence at 28 weeks (20‑25%)
Multiple gestation – limited space for cephalic turn
Uterine anomalies or fibroids – mechanical obstruction
Polyhydramnios – excess fluid allows fetal movement
Placenta praevia or low‑lying placenta – prevents head descent
Fetal anomalies (e.g., hydrocephalus, spinal dysraphism) – abnormal tone or size
Maternal pelvic contraction (e.g., previous pelvic fracture) – reduced capacity

sections.p: Patients may be unaware; the presentation is usually discovered during routine antenatal visits.
b: Absence of fetal skull palpation in the lower abdomen
High fetal heart tone on Doppler because the presenting part is lower
Maternal report of unusual fetal movements (e.g., kicking higher)
In low‑resource settings, presentation may be suspected by visual inspection of the abdomen

sections.p: If ultrasound is unavailable, rely on careful abdominal palpation and a high‑quality Doppler; refer for ultrasound when possible before deciding on delivery mode.

t.b: Confirms fetal orientation, type of breech, and looks for placental location, fetal anomalies, amniotic fluid volume
Ensures fetal well‑being before any manipulation; a normal rate (110‑160 bpm) is required
Assesses uterine size, fundal height, and rules out placenta praevia by palpation

t.a: Maternal blood group and Rh typing
t.b: Needed before any invasive procedure or delivery planning

sections.p: Identify situations that demand urgent delivery or referral.
b: Sustained fetal tachycardia (>160 bpm for >10 min) or bradycardia (<110 bpm) with reduced variability
Ruptured membranes with prolapsed cord
Maternal hemorrhage or severe pre‑eclampsia
Non‑reassuring fetal status on cardiotocography despite lack of a specific breech pattern
Failed external cephalic version after two attempts

sections.p: Management balances attempts to turn the fetus with safe delivery planning.
b: External cephalic version (ECV) at 36‑37 weeks if no contraindication; success 50‑70% in low‑resource settings due to limited tocolysis and operator skill
Tocolysis with nifedipine or beta‑agonist (if available) to relax uterus during ECV

If ECV fails or is contraindicated, plan for cesarean section for frank/complete breech; consider vaginal breech delivery only for selected footling breeches, small fetus (<3.5 kg), and experienced provider
In labour, continuous fetal monitoring; avoid prolonged second stage – consider assisted delivery (e.g., Mauriceau‑Smellie‑Veit manoeuvre) only by trained staff
Administer prophylactic antibiotics for cesarean section and for prolonged rupture of membranes

sections.p: After delivery, assess both mother and neonate; counsel for future pregnancies.
b: Neonatal exam for head injury, brachial plexus palsy, and adrenal hemorrhage (especially after difficult breech delivery)
Maternal pelvic exam to document any trauma
Educate about early presentation for antenatal care in subsequent pregnancies
If a previous breech, discuss planned ECV at 36 weeks in the next pregnancy

sections.p: Conditions that may mimic or be mistaken for breech presentation.
b: Transverse lie – fetus lies horizontally; diagnosis requires ultrasound; differs by absence of a single presenting part
Shoulder dystocia – occurs in cephalic presentation; presents with failure of shoulder delivery after head emergence, not relevant to breech
A non‑reactive NST may be due to fetal sleep, maternal anemia, or equipment artefact; it still warrants immediate reassessment and possible delivery, not simple repeat after correcting anemia
Palpation of a high fundal head may be misread as a normal cephalic lie; confirm with Doppler or ultrasound before dismissing breech

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of fetal heart tones
Persistent fetal tachycardia or bradycardia with decelerations

faq.q: Can a breech baby be delivered vaginally?
faq.a: Only in selected cases (footling breech, fetal weight <3.5 kg, experienced provider, and no maternal or fetal contraindications).

faq.q: What is the main contraindication to external cephalic version?
faq.a: Placenta praevia, active labour, ruptured membranes, or fetal distress.

faq.q: Why is a high fetal heart tone heard in breech presentation?
faq.a: The presenting part is lower, so the Doppler picks up the fetal heart more directly.

exam: A 28‑week pregnant woman presents with a firm, round head high in the fundus. What is the most likely diagnosis and next step? — Identify breech presentation; arrange ultrasound to confirm type and assess for contraindications to ECV.

You are planning an ECV at 36 weeks in a district hospital without continuous fetal monitoring. What precautions are essential? — Use tocolysis, obtain informed consent, have emergency C‑section capability, and monitor fetal heart before and after the attempt.

During labour a frank breech fetus shows prolonged second stage with fetal heart decelerations. What is the immediate management? — Stop labour, call for senior obstetrician, prepare for emergency cesarean section.
A mother with a previous cesarean scar presents at 38 weeks with a footling breech. What delivery option is safest? — Offer repeat cesarean section; vaginal breech is high‑risk with uterine scar.

What are the key neonatal injuries to look for after a vaginal breech delivery? — Check for head trauma, brachial plexus palsy, and adrenal hemorrhage; assess APGAR and initiate resuscitation if needed.

Explain why shoulder dystocia is not a concern in breech delivery. — Shoulder dystocia occurs when the fetal shoulders are impacted after a cephalic head delivery; breech delivery involves delivering the hips/feet first, so the problem is delivery of the after‑coming head, not the shoulders.

A woman in labour has a breech presentation and polyhydramnios. How does polyhydramnios affect management? — Increases risk of uterine over‑distension and failed ECV; consider earlier delivery planning and monitor for cord prolapse.

What maternal condition common in East Africa would make ECV unsafe? — Placenta praevia or active ante‑partum hemorrhage, which are more prevalent with high rates of malaria‑related anemia and uterine infections.
